clinicalPearls: A high-intensity headache of abrupt onset reaching maximum severity within one minute, mimicking a ruptured aneurysm
It is fundamentally a diagnosis of exclusion made only after serious secondary causes have been ruled out
Subarachnoid haemorrhage is the priority to exclude, followed by other vascular emergencies
Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome is a common cause of recurrent thunderclap headache and must be actively sought
Other secondary causes include cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, arterial dissection, pituitary apoplexy and spontaneous intracranial hypotension
Because the primary label carries risk, a thorough vascular and cerebrospinal fluid evaluation is essential
reference.pathophysiology: Thunderclap headache reflects sudden activation of pain-sensitive intracranial structures, most dangerously by acute vascular events such as aneurysmal subarachnoid bleeding or arterial vasoconstriction. In the primary form no cause is identified despite appropriate investigation, and its mechanism is poorly understood; it may overlap with disorders of cerebrovascular tone. The clinical imperative is that the presentation is treated as a vascular emergency until secondary causes are excluded.
additionalInvestigations: Urgent non-contrast CT of the head
Lumbar puncture for xanthochromia if CT is non-diagnostic
CT or MR angiography and venography for vascular causes
MRI of the brain for apoplexy, intracranial hypotension and other lesions
Repeat vascular imaging if RCVS is suspected, as early studies can be normal
redFlags: Any focal neurological deficit or reduced conscious level
Neck stiffness or photophobia suggesting subarachnoid blood
Recurrent thunderclap episodes suggesting vasoconstriction syndrome
reference.prognosis: When secondary causes are excluded the primary form generally has a benign course, but the initial presentation always warrants urgent investigation because the dangerous mimics are time-critical.
pitfalls: Labelling a headache primary before completing vascular and cerebrospinal fluid workup
Stopping at a normal early angiogram and missing RCVS
Overlooking venous sinus thrombosis or intracranial hypotension
Failing to exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage with lumbar puncture when CT is negative
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Immediate management as a vascular emergency, with urgent non-contrast CT of the head and lumbar puncture for xanthochromia to exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage
Cerebral CT or MR angiography and venography to exclude reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome, arterial dissection, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis and pituitary apoplexy

Where reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome is suspected, treatment with a calcium channel blocker such as nimodipine, withdrawal of vasoactive drugs, and repeat vascular imaging as early studies may be normal
Symptomatic analgesia, blood pressure control and avoidance of vasoconstrictive triggers
Reassurance about the benign course once secondary causes are confidently excluded
Neurology referral and clear safety-netting to re-present urgently if headache recurs
